{"approach":"Start at the Thunder Creek Trailhead at Colonial Creek Campground on SR 20 (turn in just past milepost 130). Follow the Thunder Creek Trail roughly 6-6.7 miles to McAllister Camp, then continue past Tricouni Camp (~8 mi) and leave the maintained trail to climb the climbers' path up 'Lucky Ridge' to a bivy near the northeast corner of the lake at the toe of the Borealis Glacier (~6,000 ft). One detailed trip log (Aug. 2018) recorded 8.25 miles and 4,760 ft of gain from trailhead to this camp in about 9 hours. Note: the footbridge that once crossed Thunder Creek near McAllister Camp is gone, so the crossing is a log jam or a wade — check current park trail conditions before you go.","approach_variants":[{"baseFinding":"The base is Lucky Pass at about 7,200 ft, and the pass identifies itself by what it divides: it is the notch at the head of the Borealis Glacier between Primus and Tricouni Peak, and the route to Tricouni splits off east from the same spot. If the ground only falls away on one side of you, you are not at the pass.

From the pass the east slope rises directly west — a bouldery class 3 slope, not a ridge crest and not a face. Parties describe the climbing above the pass as nothing more than a walk, which is the honest summary: the difficulty of this route is the creek, the brushy ridge and the glacier, all of which are behind you by the time you are at the pass.

The counting test is the false summit, and it is the one thing above the pass that can go wrong. A false summit stands at about 8,270 ft. You traverse climber's-left around it — you do not go over it — and the true summit at 8,508 ft is beyond. If you reached a high point without having traversed around anything, you are 240 ft short.

Negative test against the peak's other routes, and it works before you ever leave the car: this route is the only one reached from the Thunder Creek side. The South Ridge is reached from the Eldorado ice cap across five glaciers, and the North Ridge from an unnamed glacier north of the peak. If you walked up a creek trail from a campground on Highway 20, you are on this one.","hazards":["A mandatory Thunder Creek ford with a powerful current, worse later in the day as snowmelt rises","The central icefall on the Borealis Glacier — stay on the eastern margin","Hidden crevasses that open both vertically and horizontally, and moats where snow pulls off rock, worst late season","Cloud and fog that move in on this glacier routinely","A long, remote approach with no cell coverage"],"name":"Thunder Creek and Lucky Ridge to the Borealis Glacier and Lucky Pass","notes":"Start at the Thunder Creek trailhead at Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, just past milepost 130, near 1,200 ft. Follow the Thunder Creek Trail roughly six miles to McAllister Camp, then continue past Tricouni Camp around mile eight.

A ford of Thunder Creek at a log jam is normally required and the footbridge that once crossed near McAllister Camp is gone — check current park conditions rather than assuming a dry crossing.

Total gain to the base is on the order of 2,000+ ft over roughly 2-2.5 miles one-way; plan 1.5-2.5 hours. The step gains the little-visited northwest plateau of Liberty Bell, a bench of larch groves below the northwest face proper.

So there are two confirmations and both work without seeing the summit: the step is ten feet and well-trodden, and above it you are standing on a bench with larch trees on it. Larches on a bench, on the northwest side, below a wall, is the plateau.

The negative test against the other routes off this path, which is where parties actually go wrong: if you have dropped into the gully between Liberty Bell and Concord and are climbing scree toward a notch, you are on the Beckey Route and Overexposure approach, not this one. This route never enters that gully.

Where the day ends up, which is not where it started: from the west summit you downclimb and scramble to the top of the Beckey Route line and descend that way rather than reversing the northwest face. Rope, axe and crampons go on here, not later — the crossing to Glacier Gap and then onto the White River Glacier is the whole of the day's crevasse exposure. This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling — no fixed anchors, bolts, or rappel stations are known on this route, and parties describe reversing the glacier-and-ridge line rather than any rope-lowering. The real descent hazards are glacier hazards, not rock hazards: one party found fully open crevasses low on the White Chuck Glacier requiring careful route-finding/crampon work, and a roughly 200-yard section of exposed blue ice (a shallow icefall) on the White River Glacier that demands careful crampon travel; stay roped for glacier travel on the way down as well as up, and expect snow bridges to be less trustworthy and crevasses less obvious in early season than by late summer. {"approach_variants":[{"baseFinding":"The lake is the anchor and the route is read from it. The lake sits immediately north-east of the summit, so from the water the peak is to the south-west.

Leave the lake basin and gain the broad basin and slopes on the peak's south side, aiming for the low point on the summit ridge rather than for the summit itself. There are no cairns and no path here; the terrain is the navigation.

The ground confirms itself as you gain height: loose unconsolidated talus interspersed with heather benches on a steep grade, with unstable footing and no established tread. Note your ascent line, because on the descent one talus-and-heather slope looks exactly like the next and there is nothing to follow.

The finish is the test that you chose the right side. From the ridge the last stretch to the top is a short exposed class 3 scramble. If the ground above you is a steep continuous snow line splitting the summit block, you have come round onto the north side and are under the couloir route, which is a different proposition entirely and wants an axe, crampons and a season this route does not.

Also confirm the peak: a similarly named summit elsewhere in the range is approached from a completely different valley. The lake immediately north-east of your summit is what identifies this one.","hazards":["reaching the valley at all depends on a ferry or floatplane and a shuttle","an unmarked off-trail push into the basin with no reliable path","loose unconsolidated talus and steep heather benches with unstable footing","no tread to follow on the descent, on ground where every slope looks the same","an exposed class 3 finish off the ridge","conflicting records of the approach drainage, so the departure point must be planned from maps"],"longForm":true,"name":"Up the valley from the landing, then off-trail into the lake basin","notes":"There is no road to this side of the peak. Reach the valley by ferry or floatplane, then take the valley road or the park shuttle to a campground and pick up the valley trail from there. The lake below the peak is reached by leaving that trail and pushing off-trail and unmarked into the basin - a steep, poorly marked fisherman's path at best, and map-and-compass travel above it. Figure a full day of travel each way and plan on two or three days with a camp at or below the lake.

orig: {"approach":"Primary approach is from the north via the Stuart Lake Trailhead (reached via Icicle Creek Road and FR 7601 out of Leavenworth). From the trailhead, follow the Stuart/Colchuck Lake Trail as it rolls along Mountaineer Creek through forest; at the signed junction roughly 2 miles in, stay left/straight (the Colchuck Lake fork splits right). Continue on the Mountaineer Creek/Stuart Lake trail for about another 0.2 mile, then leave the maintained trail before reaching Stuart Lake itself, cross Mountaineer Creek, and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. After roughly 2 more miles of streamside travel, climb a steep, loose talus/boulder slope to gain the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa Glacier — this valley has good bivy sites and is a common overnight stop. From the valley, angle directly up to the toe of the North Ridge, keeping the Ice Cliff Glacier on your left; the notch/base of the upper ridge sits around 8,200 ft, where a snow-filled gully (often climbed on 4th-class rock at its edge) gains the crest. All-in this is roughly 6-6.5 miles and 3,300+ ft of gain, about 4-5 hours to the base of the climbing. A well-known alternative is the southern approach via the Esmeralda/Teanaway trailhead over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, gaining the ridge from that side (~9 miles, ~4,800 ft gain, ~8 hours) — longer and higher-gain on the way in, but it sets up a much shorter car-to-car loop for parties planning to descend the Cascadian Couloir, since that descent drops back toward Ingalls Creek. Water is available at Mountaineer Creek and its south fork on the north approach, and at Ingalls Creek/seasonal snow patches near the 8,200 ft notch bivy on the south approach; above the notch there is no reliable water. Route-finding through the boulder/talus slope below Sherpa Glacier and the creek crossing (higher and faster in early season) are the main approach-specific hazards."}

{"approach_variants":[{"baseFinding":"Look at the mountain from Longs Pass and settle the line there. It is the only point on the approach where the entire south face is laid out in front of you, and once you have dropped to the valley floor at 4,800 ft the couloir's mouth is one of several timbered gully mouths that all look alike from below and from inside the trees.

What you are aiming for: the couloir bottoms out in the meadow at roughly 4,800 ft, upvalley (east) of where the Longs Pass trail meets Ingalls Creek, and a beaten climbers' path leaves the meadow directly into it. It is a wide, sandy, scree-floored trough rather than a narrow cleft, and it runs unbroken for about 4,000 ft.

The confirmation that you are in the right gully comes about two thirds of the way up: a permanent snowfield around 8,800 ft, just south of the false summit. The established talus path passes it on the climber's left. Parties who take the right-hand side of that snowfield end up on much harder ground and have found old rappel-station remnants there — that is the tell that you have gone wrong, not a sign you are on route.

The couloir does not top out on the summit. It delivers you to the false summit at about 9,200 ft; the true summit at 9,415 ft is a class 2-3 scramble east along the ridge from there, and this is the second place parties in cloud go wrong — stopping at the false summit, or dropping off it in the wrong direction on the way down.","hazards":["Sun-exposed hillside to Longs Pass with no water and no shade","Ingalls Creek can run high in early-season melt; find the summer log rather than fording blind","The couloir is loose top to bottom — sand, scree and unstable blocks; serious rockfall risk from parties above","Upper couloir braids into a maze of use-paths and cairns; genuinely confusing in cloud or at dawn/dusk","The 8,800 ft snowfield must be passed on the climber's left"],"hours":"3-4","name":"Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — summer scramble","notes":"Drive the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737) to the Esmeralda Basin road-end parking at about 4,243 ft. A quarter mile of old mining road leads to a fork; take the right branch for Longs Pass. The trail climbs an open, south-facing hillside with essentially no shade — in July and August this is a pre-dawn start, not a preference. Longs Pass sits around 6,200-6,250 ft, roughly 2,000 ft above the car in about two miles, and it is the single most useful place on the whole approach. From the pass, drop the steep loose scree on the north side, losing 1,200-1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft. Cross the creek — there is a summer log crossing, and in high melt it is worth walking to find it rather than wading — then follow the Ingalls Creek Trail upvalley (east) about a mile to the meadow and camps below the couloir's outlet. Good camps sit on the valley floor more or less straight south of where the couloir comes down, with a few more near the footlog. From camp a climbers' path threads the meadow to the toe of the couloir. This is also the standard descent for the North Ridge, West Ridge and most of the rest of Stuart, so expect to share it.","primary":true,"season":"Jul-Sep, once the couloir has melted to talus"},{"baseFinding":"With snow cover the couloir reads far more clearly from the valley than it does in summer — it is the continuous white ribbon running the full height of the south face, and the timbered gully mouths that confuse people in August are buried. Still take the look from Longs Pass, because the valley-floor approach is in trees.

The 8,800 ft snowfield that is a landmark in summer is not a distinct feature when everything is snow, so the useful marker on the way up is the false summit at about 9,200 ft where the couloir ends. Do not treat topping out as summiting; the true summit is a scramble further east along the ridge.

On the descent in these conditions the risk inverts: the couloir is a glissade or boot-ski for most of its length and parties overrun themselves. Keep the axe in hand.","hazards":["FR 9737 unmaintained in winter/spring — verify access before driving out","Avalanche exposure on the Longs Pass hillside and in the couloir itself","South-facing: wet-slide and rockfall risk build through the day, so an early turnaround is not optional","Firm/icy snow at dawn on the north side of Longs Pass","Uncontrolled glissade on descent"],"name":"Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — spring snow climb","notes":"The same line, in a completely different medium. With the couloir snow-filled it is a straightforward steep snow climb rather than a scree grind, and many parties prefer it this way — but it demands axe and crampons, an early start, and a hard turnaround, because the whole thing faces south and softens fast.

FR 9737 is a gravel road that is not maintained through winter and is generally not clear until late June in a heavy year, so a genuinely early-season attempt means adding road miles on foot or ski. Check the road before committing.

The Longs Pass hillside carries avalanche exposure in winter and spring conditions, and the north-side drop to Ingalls Creek holds snow that can be firm and icy at dawn and slushy by mid-morning.","season":"May-Jun as a snow route; road access is the limiting factor earlier"}]}

orig: {"descent_text":"There's no walk-off back down the Mowich Face itself — after topping out, the standard descent is a long carryover, either down the Emmons-Winthrop Glacier to Camp Schurman/White River, or down the Disappointment Cleaver to Paradise, both requiring a prearranged shuttle back to Mowich Lake. This is a walk-off/glacier descent, not a rappel descent; no fixed rappels are used on either standard exit. If a party needs to retreat rather than continue over the top, they reverse the approach: back down across the North Mowich Glacier, up and over the ~1,000 ft scree/talus slope near Observation Rock, and out through Spray Park to Mowich Lake, which is a long day/night hike out."}

orig: {"descent_text":"The standard descent reverses the south-ridge climbers' trail back down to Virgin Lake and out Blanca Lake Trail #1052 to the trailhead — this is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel descent, and there are no fixed anchors or rap stations reported anywhere on the route. That said, multiple trip reports flag the crux as happening on the way down, not up: downclimbing the summit block and a short, exposed 4th-class knife-edge section reads noticeably harder in the downhill direction, and the faint climbers' trail below the ridge is easy to lose in the brushy traverse back toward Virgin Lake — budget extra time for route-finding here. Some parties carry a rope and rig a single improvised rappel off a natural anchor (sling around a rock horn or block — no bolts or fixed gear reported) to protect the summit-block downclimb or the knife-edge crux, particularly with a less-experienced party or in wet/icy conditions; treat this as optional protection for one short pitch rather than a required multi-rappel descent, so a single 30-60m rope is more than sufficient if you bring one. Several reports instead recommend descending via the Columbia Glacier as faster and more enjoyable than fighting the brushy climbers' trail, conditions permitting (visible, avoidable crevasses and a not-too-broken-up glacier); if you go that way, watch for crevasses on the lower apron and soft, sliding midday slush in summer snow. Some parties carry a rope and rig a single improvised rappel off a natural anchor (sling around a rock horn or block — no bolts or fixed gear reported) to protect the summit-block downclimb or the knife-edge crux, particularly with a less-experienced party or in wet/icy conditions; treat this as optional protection for one short pitch rather than a required multi-rappel descent, so a single 30-60m rope is more than sufficient if you bring one. Descending via the Columbia Glacier can be faster and more enjoyable than fighting the brushy climbers' trail, conditions permitting (visible, avoidable crevasses and a not-too-broken-up glacier); if you go that way, watch for crevasses on the lower apron and soft, sliding midday slush in summer snow. Whichever line you descend, this is commonly a long day with a probable dark finish, or plan a second night at Virgin Lake.","itinerary":{"cal":"Road and trail are typically snow-free and accessible early-to-mid summer through fall; check North Fork Sky road status and expect lingering snow on the glacier/upper ridge into July.","days":[{"gainFt":6000,"hours":11,"lossFt":6000,"miles":12,"n":1,"note":"The near-universal way this route is done: a single long day from the Blanca Lake Trailhead. orig: {"approach":"Same trailhead as the Classic Route: park at the Reflection Lake pullout on Stevens Canyon Road when it's open, or at the Narada Falls pullout in winter/spring when the road is snow-gated (a short, steep ~200 ft climb from Narada Falls regains the road). Walk the road about half a mile to the 90-degree bend, then drop south through open forest toward Tatoosh Creek (~4,500 ft), as with the Classic Route. Rather than climbing right toward the south-face saddle, stay low and work into the basin directly below Lane Peak's north face — the Zipper is the obvious left-leaning couloir splitting the center of the face, visible from the road. From the basin, hike up and across a large triangular apron of avalanche/rockfall debris fanning down from the base of the couloir. From the top of this debris cone, angle climber's left and climb roughly 1,000 ft up the couloir itself to a dead tree at a notch in the peak's east ridge, which marks the top of the technical climbing and the rappel/tie-in point. Snow conditions range from styrofoam neve to alpine ice depending on season and aspect; the basin and lower couloir cross avalanche-prone terrain, so this is a start-early, check-the-forecast approach, especially in winter/spring when most ascents happen. Total approach is roughly 2-2.5 miles one-way from the road with around 2,000+ ft of gain to the notch; no water past Tatoosh Creek. In the couloir itself, expect the angle to build from about 40° to 45° near the top, the walls narrowing from roughly 40 ft to 20 ft wide, and up to three short ice/mixed steps (about 15 ft, 8 ft, and a 25 ft crux) depending on fill."}

orig:
{"approach_variants":[{"baseFinding":"The base is the shoulder at about 5,500 ft on the divide between the White Salmon Glacier and the Price cirque, and it is confirmed by what you can see behind and below you rather than above: from the shoulder you look down onto Price Lake. If Price Lake is not below you, you have not gained the shoulder — you are still on the glacier or on its moraine, and the face above you is foreshortened enough that it will look like the start.

orig: {"descent_text":"Descend the same line used on the ascent — no rappels are required on the standard Eel Glacier/Flypaper Pass route. From the summit, reverse the class 3 scramble and the traverse across the upper Eel Glacier, working back around the rock buttress (Echo Rock) and re-crossing the bergschrund that cuts across the glacier below Flypaper Pass; the 'schrund forces an end-around to one side or the other, and there is a short (~50 ft) stretch of steep snow just above it that is worth pitching out or plunging pickets for in icy conditions. Climb back up and over Flypaper Pass, then face-in downclimb (or plunge-step/glissade if conditions allow) the steep snow finger back down toward the tarn and high camp — this finger is the real descent crux, reaching an estimated 40+ degrees in its steepest section as the season progresses; a short hand-line or an occasional rappel off a picket or natural anchor is a reasonable precaution late in the year even though it isn't part of the standard beta and most parties downclimb it unroped in good early-season snow. From high camp, retrace the West Fork Dosewallips Trail through Honeymoon Meadows, Diamond Meadows, Big Timber, and Dose Forks back to the Dosewallips Ranger Station, then out the old road and washout bypass to the trailhead. Note that parties climbing Mount Anderson's West Peak by other lines (e.g., a north-face variant) have reported rappelling off natural snow-horn anchors, but that is a different route, not this standard East Peak/Eel Glacier line."}

From Fred's Lake, follow the unmaintained middle section of the Eureka Creek Trail (or cross-country) east across the upper Eureka Creek basin - the creek crossing can be difficult when swollen with snowmelt - to reach Shellrock Basin/Shellrock Pass on the south side of the Lago-Carru ridge. Coming up from Shellrock Basin, the start is the toe of the broad south slope above the last stunted trees, at the point where heather gives out and continuous rock begins. In both cases the confirming feature is what is not there: this side carries no cliff band across it. If you are looking up at a wall rather than a long, tedious, uniform slope, you have drifted round onto the wrong aspect and should traverse back south. The mountain's real hazard sits on the far side of the crest, so the top is where care is needed rather than the base. The north side of the summit ridge is an enormous cliff, and the moment you can see straight down you have gone too far north.
